subject: Biotechnology
title: Mycoremediation
description: A fast breakdown of Mycoremediation for builders.

hook.text: Fungi break down wood — but their powerful enzymes also degrade pesticides, dyes, and even TNT explosives.

buildup.text: White-rot fungi produce lignin peroxidase and laccase — enzymes so aggressive they attack almost any organic molecule.

discovery.text: Oyster mushrooms degraded 95% of diesel oil in contaminated soil within eight weeks — outperforming bacterial bioremediation.

twist.text: Mycelial networks transport nutrients to pollution hotspots — fungi do not wait for pollution to arrive, they grow toward it.

climax.text: Mycofiltration uses fungal mats to filter polluted water — a low-tech solution for contaminated runoff in developing regions.

punchline.text: Fungi decompose the world — mycoremediation turns that power against pollution.

quiz.question: Why are white-rot fungi effective at degrading diverse pollutants?
options: They absorb pollutants into their cell walls permanently
They produce non-specific oxidative enzymes like lignin peroxidase that attack almost any organic molecule
They secrete acids that dissolve all types of chemical compounds

details.summary: Mycoremediation uses fungi, particularly white-rot fungi, to decompose persistent pollutants including petroleum hydrocarbons, pesticides, and even some plastics. Fungal enzymes like laccases and peroxidases break down complex molecular structures that bacteria cannot metabolize.
details.whyItMatters: Many persistent pollutants resist bacterial degradation but are vulnerable to fungal enzymes. Mycoremediation offers a powerful complementary bioremediation strategy, with mushroom-forming fungi that can be easily cultivated and deployed at
takeaways: White-rot fungi produce powerful enzymes that degrade persistent pollutants
Fungi can break down PAHs, pesticides, dioxins, and some synthetic polymers
Mycelium networks spread through contaminated soil, accessing pollutants directly

faq.question: How do fungi break down pollutants that bacteria cannot?
faq.answer: White-rot fungi evolved to decompose lignin, the toughest natural polymer, using non-specific oxidative enzymes. These same enzymes, including laccases and manganese peroxidases, attack the aromatic ring structures in many persistent pollutants. This non-specificity makes them versatile degraders.

faq.question: Can you just spread mushrooms on contaminated soil?
faq.answer: In practice, contaminated soil is mixed with fungal-colonized wood chips or straw that serves as food and growth substrate. The mycelium grows from this material into the contaminated soil, secreting enzymes as it spreads.
